h1: Building a beer aroma kit from your kitchen spice box
title: A Beer Aroma Kit from Your Spice Box | Craft Beer School
desc: Build a cheap beer aroma training kit from Indian kitchen ingredients: what to use for each beer aroma, how to prepare it and how to practise.
teaser: Your masala dabba already holds half the aromas in a hefeweizen. Here is how to turn it into a training kit.
standfirst: Professional aroma kits cost money and take time to arrive. An Indian kitchen holds many of the same aromas found in beer. With a few jars and an afternoon, you can build a training kit that teaches your nose to name what it smells.
sections:
Most homebrewers can tell a good beer from a bad one but struggle to say why. The missing piece is vocabulary tied to memory. When you have smelt clove next to a hefeweizen, the link sticks. Our guide to beer aroma vocabulary lists the words. A kit gives each word a smell.

Commercial kits use pure compounds at measured strengths. Nothing replaces them for faults. Kitchen ingredients are rougher, but they cover a surprising number of good beer aromas and cost almost nothing.

• 12 to 16 small glass jars with lids, such as spice jars or small jam jars.
  • Cotton wool balls or small pieces of plain kitchen paper.
  • Labels and a marker. Write a code on the lid and keep the answer list separately.
  • A neutral, light lager for the beer-based samples.

For dry ingredients, put a small amount in the jar, crushed if needed. Cover with a cotton ball so you smell rather than see it. For wet ones, put a few drops on the cotton.

• Clove (laung). The phenolic note in hefeweizen and many Belgian ales. Lightly crushed, two cloves are plenty.
  • Coriander seed (dhania). Citrus and floral, the spice in witbier.
  • Black pepper (kali mirch). The peppery note in saison yeast character and some rye beers.
  • Cinnamon (dalchini) and nutmeg (jaiphal). Winter beers and some Belgian ales.
  • Dried ginger (saunth). Spiced and herbal beers.
  • Cardamom (elaichi). Not a classic beer aroma, but useful for Indian spiced beers and a good contrast to coriander.

• Ripe banana. A slice mashed on cotton. The isoamyl acetate ester in hefeweizen.
  • Green apple peel. Similar to acetaldehyde, a sign of young or unfinished beer.
  • Jaggery or caramelised sugar. Caramel and toffee from crystal malts.
  • Toast crust and a plain biscuit. The bready, biscuity notes of pale malts.
  • Freshly ground coffee and cocoa powder. Roasted malts in stouts and porters.
  • Orange and lemon zest. Citrus hops and witbier.
  • Sweetcorn from a tin. A good stand-in for DMS. Put a little of the liquid on cotton.
  • Wet cardboard. A strip of brown cardboard soaked in water for oxidation.

Some aromas are clearer in beer. Pour a neutral lager into small glasses and add:

  • A few drops of lemon juice to learn sourness.
  • A crushed clove left for an hour to learn phenolic character in context.
  • A slice of fresh ginger or a few coriander seeds.

Make these fresh on the day and throw them away after the session. Do not drink spiked samples after a long sit at room temperature.

Pick a room without cooking smells, incense or air freshener. Skip perfume or scented hand cream that day. Smell each jar for no more than a few seconds, then rest. If your nose tires, sniff the inside of your own forearm or elbow to reset it. Keep a glass of water and a notebook beside you. Leave a minute between jars.

1. Start open: smell each labelled jar and say the word aloud.
  2. Next session, smell the coded jars blind and write down what you think each is.
  3. Check your answers and repeat the ones you missed.
  4. Then taste a real beer, such as a hefeweizen or a stout. Try to name what you smelt in the kit.

Short, frequent sessions of 10 to 15 minutes beat one long one. Refresh the jars every week or two, as ground spices lose aroma quickly in Indian heat. Practise with a friend so you can test each other.

Kitchen ingredients only approximate faults. Real diacetyl, isovaleric acid and the exact compounds behind oxidation do not live in your spice box. A banana is close to isoamyl acetate but not the same. Nobody should try to brew a fault deliberately in a home kitchen. For accurate fault training you need prepared standards such as commercial spiking kits and someone experienced to guide the session.

Our guide on training your palate suggests the next steps once the kitchen kit feels easy.
faqs: Can I really train my palate with kitchen spices?
Yes, for many of the pleasant aromas in beer such as clove, banana, citrus, caramel and roast. For faults you need commercial spiking standards.
Short sessions of 10 to 15 minutes, two or three times a week, work better than one long session.
How long do the jars last?
Refresh them every week or two. Ground spices and fresh ingredients lose aroma quickly, especially in hot weather.
Is sweetcorn a good stand-in for DMS?
It is close enough to teach the general aroma. DMS in beer smells of cooked or tinned sweetcorn, so tinned corn liquid works as a rough reference.
